item.title: Ohio State coach Ryan Day addresses NFL players returning to college football: 'We're in a different world'
item.description: Ohio State's Ryan Day calls on conferences to establish a roster lock deadline as former NFL players become eligible to play college football.
item.content:encoded:
Not everything about modern college football is perfect, but we can say this for it: it's never boring.

After an offseason dominated by debate over the importance of strength of schedule and how it's defined, the changing of the guard between the SEC and Big Ten, potential involvement from the federal government in collegiate athletics, and even more NIL (name, image and likeness) concerns, there's now a new controversy, just a few days before the season starts.

Thanks to a series of cases making their way through the courts as a result of the NCAA adding a fifth year of eligibility, several players who ended their "amateur" careers and went to the NFL are now eligible to return to the college football ranks.

NCAA ROCKED BY COLORADO JUDGE'S 2022 CLASS ELIGIBILITY RULING THAT COULD RESHAPE COLLEGE SPORTS THIS YEAR

Immediately, opportunistic coaches seized on the opportunity to add more physically developed and experienced players to their rosters. Led by new LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin.

This has led to a flood of conference calls and meetings among major conferences as to the propriety of players who signed with NFL teams being allowed to play college football. One of the most prominent voices in the sport, Ohio State Buckeyes head coach Ryan Day, added his perspective, highlighting the push and pull of factors dominating discussion.

LSU’S LANE KIFFIN FIRES BACK AT NFL RETURNEE BACKLASH: BLAME THE NCAA, NOT US FOR RECRUITING PRO ATHLETES

"I told myself I would stop saying this is crazy," Day told the media earlier this week. "So I’m not gonna say that. But to think that we’re in a situation where we’re this late in the season and our rosters are not locked in is frustrating at the very least. But I’m not gonna sit here and keep saying that. So what does that mean for us? That’s the bottom line. Well, I think, in my opinion, the conferences have to decide if there’s a point where their rosters have to be locked in. Because once some of these guys become available, adding them to the roster is going to provide advantage for certain teams. So we’re certainly having conversations. I’ve had conversations with Tony Petitti about this. I know he’s all over it and trying to do what’s best for the conference."

Those are all valid points. Rosters not being "locked in" with literally days to go before kickoff is not only crazy, it's unfair to the current players who could now be forced to compete for jobs with players who have experience in NFL training camps. Still, Day brought up that programs will have to "consider it" in order to keep up with other top teams.

NCAA CREATED THIS MESS, NOW LSU SET TO MAKE DAE’QUAN WRIGHT COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S FIRST NFL RETURNEE

"But we also, if there are teams that have some players out there who are cut from NFL rosters that are gonna be on other teams, we have to at least consider it and look at it," he added. "Do I like anything about it? Absolutely not, but we gotta do what’s right for Ohio State. So it’s sort of a day-to-day thing right now. And like anything, we’re just gonna try to adapt. But I think we would all agree, maybe not everybody, but that there has to be a certain point where your roster gets locked in."

That's the reality; if peer schools are signing NFL players, and you're not, you're falling behind. Just like you would fall behind if you're signing the 50th best recruiting class and Michigan is signing the number one recruiting class in the country. Or if you're not utilizing the transfer portal or NIL as efficiently as possible.

None of that changes the fact that it's bizarre, absurd, and ridiculous for players who have signed NFL contracts to return to college football. Which Day also acknowledged, referencing the recent headlines of Kiffin's LSU team bringing in a tight end for an NFL team.

"Whenever I heard that we were in a meeting and someone says, 'Yeah, LSU just got a commitment from the Browns’ tight end,' I said, 'we are definitely in a different world right now,'" he concluded.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

That's the reality, and it's hard to stomach. We are in a different world with college football, and it's going to take strong, consistent leadership to ensure it doesn't go too far. The bad news? As the past few years have repeatedly demonstrated, college football has anything but.

item.title: IndyCar's Freedom 250 Grand Prix may have been 'once-in-a-lifetime,' but this is why it needs to happen again
item.description: The Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington, D.C., delivered a once-in-a-lifetime spectacle with the Capitol and Washington Monument as backdrops.
item.content:encoded:
I still remember exactly where I was in late January when I got a message from an editor that President Trump was preparing to sign an executive order to bring an IndyCar race to Washington, DC.

I replied that there was no way it would happen during the 2026 season, which was only about a month away from starting at the time. The track needed to be designed, built and made safe before cars could get on it, not to mention all of the fan areas and other logistics.

But seven months later, I was on a plane to the nation's capital to see the Freedom 250 Grand Prix for myself, and, man, was I ever wrong.

WORLD CUP ENERGY CARRIES INTO FREEDOM 250 GRAND PRIX AS GLOBAL FANS CELEBRATE AMERICA'S HISTORIC BIRTHDAY

Not only did it work, but it was the once-in-a-lifetime spectacle it promised to be.

And, if there's any way, it needs to happen again.

For starters, there's really never been a backdrop like it. It was pretty awe-inspiring to see the Capitol and the Washington Monument towering over the circuit and to see every rooftop and terrace lined with people trying to get a view of the track.

The turnout on both days was incredible, and that, of course, is largely due to the fact that tickets were free. It was an unbeatable deal, even if the merch was not the cheapest I've ever seen.

I bought an event poster that I thought would be like $10, and it was $60 because it was printed on canvas.

That said, the food was fairly affordable, with the priciest thing I saw being a crab cake sandwich for $25. It's not a deal, but you won't have to skip a mortgage payment for a burger like you might at an F1 race.

One critique would be that they needed more screens around the track. Especially when you consider the nature of a street circuit, you really can't have too many screens. I believe I counted four in the one fan area on the National Mall, and none if you were watching from the outside part of the track.

That's a bit of a problem, because as anyone who has been to a street race can tell you, it can sometimes be hard to see a lot of the track.

There also wasn't a ton to do in the way of fan activations as you see at a lot of other races, but you could access the museums within the track, including the National Air and Space Museum.

I spent a good chunk of time in the fan area on the National Mall walking around and talking to fans, and it almost had a county fair vibe to it, which I mean in the best way possible.

Everyone I encountered seemed happy to be there, and I never saw politics come up once. In fact, most of the people OutKick's Jon Root and I talked to were happy that politics were taking a backseat to good old-fashioned American pride and racing, a sentiment shared by fans we spoke to from as far away as the UK and Norway.

If the monuments, landmarks, flyovers, and racing couldn't make you proud to live in the United States, I'm not sure anything could.

TRUMP TAKES HONORARY LAP AROUND INDYCAR TRACK IN WASHINGTON AHEAD OF FREEDOM 250 GRAND PRIX

Some fans we spoke to admitted that they didn't have the first clue about IndyCar, and I think that may be one of the greatest victories of this event for the series.

Nothing will get someone hooked on motorsports faster than attending a race. It’s hard to explain to nonfans why those of us who love the sport spend most Sundays watching cars go in circles.

You can explain strategies, technology and how important a battle for P8 in the standings is, but it just won't click.

But if you take someone to a race and they can see the cars, hear the cars and even smell, in this case, the Firestone rubber getting left behind on Pennsylvania Avenue, well, that's going to make them a fan faster than any broadcast ever could.

That was the experience thousands of people got on Sunday. They may not have taken the Metro out of DC talking about whether or not Scott McLaughlin should've gone for the race-winning move into Turn 1 on a restart with 20 laps left (I think he should've slipstreamed down Pennsylvania Ave. and tried into Turn 2), but they will, without a doubt, tune into races in the future.

The track itself turned out to be great, something I was not expecting. When it was unveiled, I remember being pretty underwhelmed by its seven corners, all but one of which was 90 degrees or close to it.

However, the early maps didn't make it clear that Turn 6 was one heck of a chicane, and the bumpy street circuit proved to be a challenge for drivers.

And, on top of that, overtaking was possible.

Plus, despite Kyle Kirkwood dominating the weekend, I thought the race was really entertaining. We got a good strategic battle with the frontrunners using the early caution to pull off a three-stopper, and the late cautions giving us some important restarts.

That extra race distance was a good call, and I'm sure everyone there went home feeling like they got their money's worth... even if their ticket was free.

The free tickets to the Freedom 250 Grand Prix were one of the coolest parts of the event, but if it's going to become a sustainable addition to the IndyCar calendar, that might need to change.

The city showed that it was capable of making it all work from a logistical perspective, but ticket revenue sure would help keep the lights on.

They did charge for premium ticket options, which helped pay for part of the event, with Penske Corporation paying for the rest. That means no taxpayer dollars were involved (sorry, Adam Schiff!).

Everything else was general admission, including the grandstands, which were first-come, first-served.

I think the solution would be to add a grandstand or two and charge standard IndyCar ticket prices to sit in those seats, but then maybe hold another free ticket lottery that lets people get in and watch from trackside.

While there may be a few details that would need a second look if the powers that be decide to run it back with Freedom 250 Grand Prix 2.0, I was really impressed by how smoothly everything went.

If IndyCar never hits the streets of Washington again, it will be really neat to tell people that you were there to see it happen.

But the event has the makings of a signature IndyCar race on a big scale, and that’s something the series needs. That’s what gets eyeballs on the sport and converts people into fans, as was on display this weekend.

Imagine a schedule with marquee races like the Grand Prix of Arlington, the Grand Prix of Long Beach, the Indianapolis 500 and a race around Washington, D.C.?

That would be something to behold and, given the reception, perhaps someday soon we’ll get to see it.

item.title: Massive fishing boat runs aground at popular beach with 1,000 gallons of diesel on board
item.description: A 58-foot fishing boat ran aground at North Beach in Northern California's Point Reyes National Seashore, triggering a closure and diesel removal effort.
item.content:encoded:
A 58-foot fishing boat ran aground at a popular Northern California beach — prompting a closure as crews worked to remove roughly 1,000 gallons of diesel from the vessel.

The Lake Bay became stranded early Friday at North Beach in Point Reyes National Seashore, according to an alert from the National Park Service (NPS).

The boat was carrying 40,000 pounds of squid at the time, Inverness resident Richard James told the Point Reyes Light, a local newspaper, citing a conversation with the vessel's skipper.

TSUNAMI OF SEWAGE FROM MEXICO BARRELS TOWARD US COASTLINE, OFFICIALS WARN

As crews began responding to the grounding, the park service announced the temporary closing of North Beach and North Beach Road.

No injuries, fuel leaks or impacts to wildlife were reported, the agency said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the NPS for further comment and details.

The Lake Bay can hold up to 2,800 gallons of fuel. It was reported to have approximately 1,000 gallons of diesel on board, according to a press release from the U.S. Coast Guard.

Crews were coordinating with the party responsible for the vessel and a contracted salvage company to remove the fuel, the Coast Guard said.

75-FOOT BOAT SURFS WAVE, RUNS AGROUND IN HAWAII

Capt. Jack Moran, owner of Sea Tow Cape May in New Jersey, told Fox News Digital that access and timing can pose challenges when dealing with a grounded vessel. 

"The biggest thing is going to be accessibility," Moran said, noting that crews have to contend with tides, currents and changing conditions. "Time is the enemy. You want to try and get it off there as quickly as possible." (He is not connected to or involved with the Lake Bay fishing boat.) 

With 40,000 pounds of squid reportedly onboard, Moran said removing the catch could present another challenge.

"Moving a product like that is challenging at a dock, let alone removing squid from a boat on a beach," he said.

For the Coast Guard, safety and environmental concerns remained at the center of the response.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Our top priorities are ensuring the safety of the first responders and the public, stabilizing the incident, and limiting environmental impacts," Lt. Cmdr. Carey Lewis, the Coast Guard incident commander, said in the release. 

"Responders are continuously monitoring and evaluating the site for pollution and any potential risk factors so we can approach operations with [an] intention to minimize environmental impacts."

The National Park Service asked visitors to stay away from North Beach while the closure is in effect to allow first responders to work safely.

The cause of the grounding remains under investigation, the Coast Guard said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Fox News Digital previously reported on another grounding in April involving a small cruise ship near Monuriki Island in Fiji, where the Tom Hanks movie "Cast Away" was filmed.

The Blue Lagoon Cruises vessel struck a reef after worsening weather caused its anchor to drag.

A high-speed ferry arrived around dawn to assist with the evacuation, allowing all passengers and non-essential crew members to leave the stranded ship with their belongings.

Passengers were taken back to Port Denarau, where the cruise line arranged hotel accommodations and alternative activities. No injuries were reported among passengers or crew.

Jessica Mekles of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

item.title: Charles Barkley says WNBA players 'just don't like' Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham
item.description: Charles Barkley says WNBA players dislike Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, blaming a mix of jealousy, race, and sexuality for the hostility.
item.content:encoded:
Charles Barkley didn’t mince words while talking about Indiana Fever stars Caitlin Clark, Sophie Cunningham and the WNBA.

"Those girls do not like Caitlin Clark or Sophie Cunningham," Barkley said, referring to the other players in the WNBA and their feelings toward two of the league’s most popular players. But Barkley didn’t think it was all about race.

"Without regard for race, they just don’t like them," Barkley added.

Barkley made those comments on "The Michael Smerconish Program" while the two discussed what Barkley called the WNBA’s "awful year." One of the incidents the pair talked about was DiJonai Carrington’s Flagrant 2 foul on Cunningham during the Aug. 8 game between the Fever and Chicago Sky.

WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT

Carrington delivered a vicious blow to Cunningham's head as the Fever guard attempted a fast-break layup. Cunningham was left with a bloody mouth following the contact. Referees reviewed the play, upgraded the call from a Flagrant 1 to a Flagrant 2 and ejected Carrington.

Shortly after her ejection, Carrington posted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" on social media and tagged the Fever. She later said she never claimed the Flagrant 2 itself was the result of white privilege, though she didn't explain what prompted the post.

Cunningham called the foul "unnecessary," said she had "no beef" with Carrington, then called it intentional and accused Carrington of seeking attention.

Smerconish said he went looking for data on whether hard fouls between Black and White WNBA players occur more often than they should. He said he found a peer-reviewed study suggesting they happen at the rate one would expect, which led him to argue that the media is what turns those incidents into racial controversies.

Barkley didn’t buy it.

"No, no, you’re wrong, though," Barkley said. "The reason they made it black and white [was] when that girl tweeted ‘white privilege.’ That was stupid on her part."

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT AGAINST DIJONAI CARRINGTON AFTER FLAGRANT FOUL AND 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST

Barkley called it "a dirty play. Period." He said Carrington’s post turned it into a racial argument.

"When you turn stuff to the internet, all the race hustlers start coming out. We have a ton of race hustlers out there, White and Black. Let me repeat that. White and Black," Barkley said.

Smerconish then brought up Larry Bird and Magic Johnson, whose rivalry came with obvious racial undertones but helped turn the NBA into a massive national product. Barkley agreed those undertones existed. He said the difference was that Bird and Johnson respected each other.

"There was always respect," Barkley said, before repeating himself for emphasis. "There was always respect."

Barkley didn't accuse Carrington, or any other WNBA player, of racism. He did, however, offer his own theory for the hostility toward Clark and Cunningham.

"I’m not gonna get on here and call somebody a racist because I don’t have any proof," Barkley said. "Whether it’s race, sexuality, or whatever, there’s something going on there."

He said Clark and Cunningham are simply good players, but he believes the resentment toward them comes from a mix of factors.

"She’s just a really good basketball player. Same thing with Sophie. She’s a good player," Barkley said. "I think it has something to do with sexuality, race, and jealousy. I think it’s all three of them. I don’t know how you break up the percentages."

Barkley said the WNBA’s bad publicity bothers him because he believes the league has a lot going for it. The WNBA is expanding, players are making more money under a new CBA, and the league has young stars who should be driving the conversation.

Instead, Barkley said, the WNBA keeps finding itself wrapped up in hard fouls, social-media posts and arguments that have little to do with basketball.

Smerconish suggested the WNBA could benefit from the attention, invoking the old belief that there is no such thing as bad publicity. Barkley didn’t agree.

"I don’t think it works like that anymore, Michael," Barkley said. "When’s the last time you heard something positive about the WNBA? I can’t even remember."

item.title: Kyle Shanahan breaks 49ers silence on Jed York arrest, says he still has 'respect' for the club owner
item.description: Kyle Shanahan says Jed York's arrest in an Ohio prostitution sting has no effect on the San Francisco 49ers as a team heading into the season.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers said they weren't going to comment about owner Jed York getting caught up in a prostitution sting over the weekend because the legal matter is closed , but that policy collapsed in coach Kyle Shanahan's first press conference since the incident.

Shanahan became the first 49ers official to face questions, and he felt obliged to provide answers.

(Dude is a saint).

Shanahan said York's arrest and ensuing no-contest plea to misdemeanor disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools charges in a deal with an Ohio prosecutor has no effect on the Bay Area football team.

MORE DETAILS EMERGE ABOUT JED YORK'S ARREST IN PROSTITUTION STING

"My view is, as the coach, does it have effect on us as a team?" Shanahan said. "And that's what I continue to answer on from a football standpoint. It has no effect on us. I mean, as far as what we do day to day, what we talk about, it hasn't been mentioned in a meeting today. It doesn't have to do with what happens on the field."

Shanahan, who was involved in a head-on collision in July that affected how much he was on the field early in training camp, doesn't believe that or York's legal trouble will distract the football team in the upcoming season.

"Well, the one thing that went on yesterday I don't think pertained to our players much," Shanahan said. "And if you guys talk about me getting in a car accident, I think that's kind of a joke that people think that's a distraction to our team.

"So I think it's been training camp as usual."

49ERS COACH KYLE SHANAHAN ADMITS HE CAUSED CAR CRASH AFTER TAKING EYES OFF ROAD TO FIND HIS PHONE

This, of course, is a head coach's spin on an uncomfortable situation. The majority owner of the team spent a day in jail and was splashed across national headlines because, police documents say, he went on a website in Ohio and tried to enlist the services of a prostitute on Sunday.

Three times.

And he got caught because what he was actually doing was connecting with an operation run by the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force, which arrested him with the help of East Palestine police.

NFL EMPLOYEES’ TROUBLING DRIVING INCIDENTS MOUNT, COSTING JOBS AND PUTTING OTHERS AT RISK

Despite those details, Shanahan said he has not changed his opinion about the club's owner or his family.

"Obviously, it's a very tough situation," Shanahan admitted after saying he has spoken to York the last two days. "I mean, the views for the organization going forward is the same as usual. There won't be any difference in that.

"But I know it's extremely fresh. I think it's a very, very personal situation. I got a lot of respect for Jed. I got a lot of respect for Danielle. Their family does mean a lot to me. So I'm like, you know, with it being a personal [matter], I'm trying as hard as I can to keep it that way."

Danielle Belluomini is York's wife of 15 years, but even the marriage has become a newsworthy drama. Multiple reports have cited a divorce petition filed by York almost four months ago with the reason for the break being "irreconcilable differences."

NFL owners are scheduled to gather on Wednesday to vote on the sale of the Seattle Seahawks and the York situation will almost definitely be discussed in some capacity. The league released a statement on Monday saying it is aware of York's situation, and he is subject to discipline under its Personal Conduct Policy.

So, whether Shanahan admits it or not, the football team could be affected if York is disciplined and that rises to a suspension or even removal — the latter of which is not likely but cannot be ruled out.

None of that is a concern right now for the coach, and he believes his players aren't moved by the publicity of York's troubles.

"That's what these guys deal with their whole careers," Shanahan said. "I got cameras on all the time. They got cameras in their face right after games, when they're not feeling right or something very emotional could have happened.

"I feel something like this is actually easier for them than some of the stuff they have to deal with in the heat of battle of things that are more personal to themselves."

item.title: Enes Kanter Freedom barred from Sky arena after altercation with Natasha Cloud, team owner says
item.description: Chicago Sky team owner Michael Alter said Tuesday Enes Kanter Freedom is barred from Wintrust Arena after his altercation with Natasha Cloud on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Sky team owner Michael Alter said Tuesday Enes Kanter Freedom is banned from Wintrust Arena after his altercation with Natasha Cloud on Sunday.

Alter made the comments in an address to beat writers.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"He has demonstrated to us, unequivocally, that he has the potential to be a threat," Alter said, via ESPN.

The incident occurred in the third quarter of the Sky’s loss to the Indiana Fever. Cloud scored a bucket that led to the Fever calling a timeout. She directed her emotion toward Freedom, who was sitting near the basket at the Wintrust Arena. Freedom stood up and walked toward Cloud. Sky players and security had to get in between the two.

Freedom was escorted out of the arena and was unable to return for the rest of the game.

Cloud didn’t speak at the Sky’s postgame media availability. She fired off a message on Threads in support of the transgender community.

"To every trans kid/person, You are apart of MY community & tribe. You belong. You’re loved. You’re seen. You’re perfect as you are. & you will always be protected by me," Cloud wrote.

Cloud’s message appeared to be a swipe at Freedom, who announced his intentions to compete in the WNBA as players and coaches have spoken out about trans athletes in women and girls’ sports. Freedom was wearing a T-shirt with the definition of a woman on it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Woman – adult human female," his shirt read.

Freedom later told OutKick he believed his T-shirt had something to do with the altercation.

"I was cheering for my friend Sophie because when she shot that three, I put my hands in the air," Freedom said. "A couple possessions later, she came back and said, ‘She’s not gonna sleep with you.’ And I was shocked. I was like, ‘Listen, I’m not trying to sleep with her. I think she’s awesome. She’s a good friend.’ But I think it has a lot to do with my shirt.

"I was obviously wearing a shirt explaining what a woman is, and I think that had a lot to do with what she thinks about women. I think it triggered her a lot."

Freedom attended his first WNBA game after saying he wanted to join the WNBA. As he entered the arena Sunday afternoon, he was berated by a mob of angry WNBA fans.

He has since maintained he will pursue entering the WNBA Draft.

item.title: Best hiking trails near Scott Stadium in Charlottesville: a guide for Virginia football fans
item.description: Before the Cavaliers kick off at Scott Stadium, explore Humpback Rocks, the Blue Hole swimming spot, and Shenandoah National Park all within 35 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Week 0 | NC State at Virginia | Saturday, Aug. 29 | Scott Stadium, Charlottesville, VA | 3:30 p.m. ET

Funny how things work out. This game was supposed to be college football's first trip to South America, with NC State and Virginia set to kick off Week 0 at Nilton Santos Stadium in Rio de Janeiro. Then the whole thing fell apart this summer when Athlete Advantage (the event organizer) told the ACC it simply couldn't pull it off. So the Wolfpack and Cavaliers got rerouted back to the far less exotic — but far more practical — Blue Ridge foothills of Charlottesville instead.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

Virginia's loss of a trip to Rio is your gain. Instead of fighting for a spot on a flight to Brazil, you can be standing on a mountaintop overlooking the Shenandoah Valley by 9 a.m. and in your tailgate spot by 1. Charlottesville sits right up against the Blue Ridge Parkway and the edge of Shenandoah National Park, which means some of the best hiking in Virginia is closer to Scott Stadium than most fans realize.

Here's where to go — all within an hour of kickoff and none requiring a passport or conversational Portuguese.

10 minutes from Scott Stadium | Easy

The one to bring the whole crew, including grandparents and strollers. A 4.4-mile out-and-back on packed gravel and raised boardwalk, climbing gently through forest canopy up to the visitor center at Thomas Jefferson's Monticello. Dog-friendly, wheelchair-accessible and shaded most of the way.

If anyone in your group wants to actually tour the house, that's a separate ticket — $23 to $30 for adults, $10 for kids 5 to 11 — but the trail itself is free.

30 minutes from Scott Stadium | Easy

A change of pace from the usual mountain-view hike: a 4.6-mile out-and-back through an actual 1850s railroad tunnel carved straight through the mountain under Rockfish Gap. Bring a flashlight or headlamp — it gets really dark in there, and the temperature drops the deeper you go, which is an added bonus.

BEAT THE HEAT: HERE ARE SOME OF THE BEST TIPS TO AVOID HEATSTROKE DURING A HIKE THIS SUMMER

25 minutes from Scott Stadium | $30 per vehicle | Moderate

If you're only going to spend money on one thing this weekend besides the game, this is the one worth it. The Rockfish Gap entrance drops you right onto Skyline Drive, with two standout hikes an easy detour apart: Calvary and Chimney Rocks at milepost 90, a short trek out to a flat-topped rock overlook, and Turk Mountain at milepost 93.5, which delivers rock scrambles and real mountain views for the effort.

Being a national park, it will cost you an entry fee of $30 per vehicle, which is good for seven days.

35 minutes from Scott Stadium | Moderate

The pick if you’re looking to do a little soaking. A 3-mile out-and-back from the Sugar Hollow parking area leads to the Blue Hole, a genuinely beautiful swimming hole on the Moormans River. This spot keeps showing up on the "best swimming holes in Virginia" lists for a reason. Bring water shoes; the rocks get slick.

If your crew wants more of a workout instead, a separate 4.6-mile route from the same lot heads out to Big Branch Falls through a shaded forest.

30 minutes from Scott Stadium | Moderate-strenuous

The payoff hike, and the one most worth setting an alarm for. It's a brutal, steep mile straight up, but the reward is a 360-degree view across the Shenandoah Valley and Blue Ridge that's tough to beat anywhere in the state. This is the one hike on the list with zero shade at the top, so this is the one to knock out at sunrise, not after brunch. Sunrise at Humpback is a bucket-list item for many UVA students.

60–75 minutes from Scott Stadium | $3 day-use fee | Moderate-strenuous

Crabtree Falls is a series of five major cascades tumbling a total of 1,200 feet down the mountainside. For context, that's taller than the Eiffel Tower. And the longest single cascade in that series drops 400 feet, enough to make Crabtree Falls the tallest single vertical-drop waterfall east of the Mississippi. The hike up alongside it is a 3-mile round trip with switchbacks and handrails at the steeper spots. It's genuinely one of the most photographed trails in Virginia.

The catch: this one runs 60 to 75 minutes from Scott Stadium depending on route and traffic. If you're rolling into Charlottesville just for the game, Crabtree probably isn't the move. But if you're making a weekend of it and have an extra day before or after, it's worth the drive.

We should probably also mention there's another Crabtree Falls off the Blue Ridge Parkway in North Carolina. Make sure you're plugging the right one into your GPS.

Truthfully, you can't go wrong no matter which trail you choose. Between the Blue Ridge Parkway, Shenandoah National Park and a reservoir system that seems to have a trail wrapped around every corner of it, Charlottesville is about as good as it gets for outdoor adventurers who also happen to love college football.

Every week this season, OutKick OutDoors is finding the best ways to touch grass before you touch down at the tailgate. Got a favorite spot near your campus we should know about? Hit us up on Instagram and TikTok.

item.title: Georgia redistricting battle revived after appeals court overturns federal court decision
item.description: The 11th Circuit said Georgia’s 2021 redistricting maps must be reevaluated under the Supreme Court’s newly clarified racial-discrimination standard.
item.content:encoded:
Georgia secured a major victory Tuesday in its long-running redistricting battle after a federal appeals court overturned a lower court ruling that the state’s 2021 maps violated the Voting Rights Act, sending the case back for a complete re-evaluation.

The 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said the lower court must determine whether there was a "strong inference" that the maps were intentionally drawn to dilute Black voting power, rather than simply finding that the maps had a discriminatory effect under permissible partisan gerrymandering.

The decision follows a major Supreme Court ruling in a similar Louisiana case that significantly modified the legal framework for determining racial discrimination in redistricting. The high court said plaintiffs must provide evidence of "present-day intentional racial discrimination."

"Plaintiffs must be able to show that voters are engaged in racial-bloc voting because of race, not partisan affiliation," the ruling stated.

BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES

In 2023, a federal judge ruled that Georgia’s congressional and state legislative maps drawn after the 2020 census violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and issued a permanent injunction barring Georgia from using the maps in future elections.

The lower court specifically ordered the state to create additional majority-Black districts across the state Senate, state House of Representatives and U.S. congressional districts.

Meanwhile, a similar redistricting battle was unfolding in Louisiana, where Robinson v. Ardoin challenged the state’s congressional map, which initially included just one majority-Black district out of six.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS ALABAMA REDISTRICTING PLAN IN BLOW TO TRUMP

A federal court later ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, ordering Louisiana to create a second majority-Black district after finding that the original map violated the Voting Rights Act.

However, a group of non-minority voters later challenged the new map, arguing that the newly created district amounted to racial gerrymandering and violated the 14th and 15th Amendments.

In the second lawsuit, Louisiana v. Callais, the Supreme Court ultimately upheld the constitutionality of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act while clarifying how courts should evaluate claims of racial discrimination in redistricting. The ruling emphasized the need for evidence supporting a "strong inference" of intentional discrimination, rather than relying solely on the effects of a map.

WHY THE SUPREME COURT GUTTED THE VOTING RIGHTS ACT AFTER SIX DECADES IN A BLOW TO BLACK POLITICIANS

The decision also altered the legal framework federal courts have used for decades to evaluate racial vote-dilution claims. Established in the Supreme Court’s 1986 ruling in Thornburg v. Gingles, the Gingles framework generally did not require plaintiffs to prove that lawmakers acted with racial intent and instead focused on whether a voting system had discriminatory effects.

The Georgia case will now return to the district court for reconsideration under the Supreme Court’s framework established in Louisiana v. Callais.

item.title: Deadly measles outbreak hits Northeast as state records first deaths in 35 years
item.description: Two unvaccinated Lancaster County residents died from measles, marking Pennsylvania's first measles deaths in 35 years amid 393 confirmed cases.
item.content:encoded:
Pennsylvania confirmed two measles-related deaths on Tuesday, according to the state’s department of health.

This marks the first losses related to the highly contagious virus within the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania in 35 years.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed that both Lancaster County individuals were unvaccinated, noting that the best way to prevent measles infection is to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.

MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL

The MMR vaccine administered over two doses can boost a person’s immune system and provide 97% lifetime protection, according to health officials.

In a press release, Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen shared her "deepest sympathies" with the "loved ones who are facing this unimaginable loss."

"Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness," she said in the statement. "We want to ensure that every Pennsylvanian has the information they need to protect themselves, their loved ones and their communities."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles."

The state's DOH has confirmed 393 cases of measles in 28 counties so far in 2026.

Measles is a highly contagious virus that can be fatal in one to three patients per 1,000 cases, data shows.

The virus can cause long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling. Nearly 20% of individuals who contract measles are hospitalized.

Measles spreads when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, spreading the virus through respiratory droplets. It can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the person leaves the area, experts caution.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Early measles symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A measles rash follows a few days later, starting on the head and spreading down to the rest of the body.

Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure. Those who believe they were exposed to measles should contact a healthcare provider.

Dr. Jesse Goodman, former FDA chief scientist in Washington, D.C., spoke with Fox News Digital about the MMR vaccine, calling it "extremely safe and highly effective."

"The vaccine prevents millions of measles deaths worldwide annually, including hundreds that used to occur in the U.S.," he said. "There is no evidence that MMR vaccine causes any chronic illnesses, including autism."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Dr. Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security in Baltimore, Maryland, agreed that Pennsylvania's 35-year streak without a measles-related death "wasn't luck."

"It was the vaccine working so completely that an entire generation of parents grew up never seeing what this virus does to a child’s lungs or brain," he told Fox News Digital. "That protection is increasingly not valued, and this is the predictable result when the population turns their back on a life-saving technology."

Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, previously emphasized the highly contagious nature of measles amid elevated case counts across the U.S.

"Measles is so contagious that up to 90% of susceptible people who are exposed to an infected person will become infected," he told Fox News Digital, stressing the importance of community protection. "We need a 95% vaccine coverage rate to ensure herd immunity," he said.

The herd immunity threshold is a mathematical estimate based on how contagious a disease is and how effectively immunity from vaccination or prior infection prevents its spread, according to Siegel.

"In this case, two-dose vaccination is almost 100% effective, and natural immunity after a measles infection is generally lifelong," the doctor said. "This isn’t about personal choice, it’s about community protection. We need to protect those who can’t have a live virus vaccine because they are immunocompromised or pregnant."

item.title: STEVE DOOCY: The Dolly Parton I saw when the cameras stopped rolling
item.description: Steve Doocy reflects on interviewing Dolly Parton half a dozen times, revealing the professionalism and kindness she showed when cameras weren't rolling.
item.content:encoded:
On August 23, 2016, ten years ago this week, I was with Dolly Parton in New York City, and we were about to do a live segment on FOX & Friends.

Just before we went on, I asked Dolly if I could take a selfie with her.

She looked at me and said, "Why would you want a picture with little ol’ me?"

DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80 AS COUNTRY MUSIC WORLD MOURNS BELOVED ICON WHOSE SONGS SHAPED GENERATIONS

I laughed and said, "Hello…Dolly—you’re Dolly Parton!"

That was Dolly.

Over my years on "FOX & Friends," I was lucky enough to interview her probably half a dozen times. And here’s something people watching at home wouldn’t necessarily know: Dolly was always on time. Always prepared. Always a professional.

In morning television, where guests sometimes arrive moments before they’re supposed to be on live TV—or occasionally after—that matters!

Dolly showed up ready to go. And the minute the camera came on, so did that Dolly magic.

She was funny, quick, kind and incredibly smart. She knew exactly what she wanted to say, but somehow never let an interview feel rehearsed. You could ask her a serious question and get a thoughtful answer, then a few seconds later she’d say something hilarious that nobody saw coming.

DOLLY PARTON'S CALIFORNIA RETREAT WITH WIG ROOM AND DOLLYWOOD BIRDHOUSE LISTS FOR $1.95M

She was simply great television.

But what I remember most is that she was just as nice when the cameras weren’t rolling.

Underneath the rhinestones, the big hair and that unmistakable Tennessee voice was a very savvy businesswoman. Dolly didn’t just build a career. She built an empire. She understood her audience, understood her brand and, most importantly, understood people. And somehow, through all that enormous success, she remained remarkably down-to-earth.

A few years ago, I interviewed Dolly and my friend James Patterson about the novel they wrote together, "Run, Rose, Run". Later, when I toured James’ Florida home, he showed me one of his prized possessions: a guitar Dolly had given him, inscribed with a birthday message that ended, naturally, "I will always love you."

That was Dolly, too.

And there’s another connection I had completely forgotten until today. During the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge craze in 2014, Kenny Rogers was challenged by Lionel Richie. Kenny then nominated three people to go next: Garth Brooks, Dolly Parton…and me.

To this day, I’m still not entirely sure how Steve Doocy wound up on a list with Garth Brooks and Dolly Parton—but I’m glad I did!

Dolly was one of those rare people who seemed to be exactly the same person when the cameras were off as when they were on.

Funny. Kind. Smart. Professional. And completely original.

She wrote songs that generations know by heart. She became a legendary entertainer, songwriter and businesswoman. She gave away millions of books to children. And she never seemed to forget where she came from—or lose her wonderful ability to laugh at herself.

For all her fame, Dolly always seemed to understand something important: being nice to people doesn’t cost a thing.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

I’m grateful our paths crossed so many times. And today, ten years later, I’m especially grateful I asked for that selfie.

Godspeed, Dolly.

Thanks for the music, the laughs, the memories—and the kindness.

There will never be another one quite like you.

item.title: Secret Service aware of Iranian video threat targeting Barron Trump, agency says
item.description: A video aired on Iranian state media depicts locations tied to Barron Trump and offers a suggested $10 million reward for his exact location.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Secret Service said it was aware of a video aired on Iranian state media threatening President Trump's youngest son, Barron Trump.

"The U.S. Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees," Nate Herring, a Secret Service spokesperson, told Fox News Digital.

"Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence," Herring added.

TRUMP HAS BECOME AMERICA'S MOST TARGETED LEADER, FACING THREATS EVERY FEW MONTHS

The video depicts locations associated with the younger Trump's whereabouts. It ends with a suggested $10 million reward for his location.

Iranian state media has aired content on multiple occasions threatening Trump and his family following the assassination of Iran's Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, which came at the start of the war between the United States and Iran, as well as the U.S. airstrike that killed Iranian General Qasem Soleimani in 2020.

ISRAEL SHARES INTELLIGENCE WARNING IRAN PLOTTED NEW ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT AGAINST TRUMP: REPORT

"I don't think it's any secret, it's been in the media, that Iran has publicly said they want to kill President Trump," Deputy Director of the U.S. Secret Service Matt Quinn told reporters at an event last month.

The video came amid threats from the Trump administration to nations that fail to sever their economic ties with Tehran and an ongoing naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

In July, Trump secretly switched planes from Air Force One to another aircraft in Turkey via a catering truck due to a credible Iranian surface-to-air missile threat.

The White House referred any questions about the matter to the Secret Service.

item.title: Globetrotting sailor nabbed in Canada over alleged child sex crimes aboard sailboat: FBI
item.description: Donald Steven Lang, 62, was arrested in Canada after the FBI warned the alleged child predator could be sailing across the Pacific to evade authorities.
item.content:encoded:
An alleged child predator accused of exploiting a child aboard his sailboat was arrested in Canada, after the FBI warned he could be sailing across the Pacific Ocean to evade authorities.

Donald Steven Lang, 62, was taken into custody over the weekend at the request of the United States, federal authorities said Tuesday, ending a far-reaching search for the globe-trotting sailor.

Lang, a dual U.S. and Canadian citizen, was indicted Aug. 20 in Hawaii on one count of sexual exploitation of children.

'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' FUGITIVE CAPTURED ON SAILBOAT OFF NJ COAST AFTER 20 YEARS ON THE RUN

Prosecutors allege he exploited a minor between September and December 2024 aboard his 55-foot sailboat, Ishi.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) said Lang was known to sail around the world and frequently harbored in Hawaii. But the FBI’s search for him extended far beyond the islands.

'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' FUGITIVE LAID BLUEPRINT FOR VANISHING BEFORE 20-YEAR ESCAPE: AFFIDAVIT

The bureau warned Lang, who was last seen on board Ishi in Hawaii in January 2025, could have been sailing between Hawaii and Fiji or Mexico, headed toward Papua New Guinea, or possibly Indonesia. He had ties or connections in Hawaii, Idaho, Washington state, California, Fiji, the Marquesas Islands, Mexico and Canada, the FBI said.

Federal prosecutors allege that Lang attempted to and knowingly used, persuaded, induced, enticed or coerced a minor to engage in sexually explicit conduct for the purpose of producing visual depictions.

The indictment identifies his sailboat as a 55-foot, 1985 Taylor Hatfield oceangoing sailing vessel.

Prosecutors are seeking forfeiture of the boat, digital devices and storage media, including a Samsung Galaxy S22 Ultra phone, should Lang be convicted.

'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' EX-COP FUGITIVE RETURNED AFTER 20 YEARS ON THE RUN TO FACE MURDER, CHILD SEX CHARGES

Lang was already wanted in Idaho in a separate child sex abuse case, authorities said.

Kootenai County prosecutors charged Lang in April 2025 with three counts of lewd conduct towards a minor under 16 and one count of sexual battery of a minor in connection with allegations that he sexually assaulted a minor between 2003 and 2007.

MORE THAN 300 ARRESTED IN SPRAWLING CALIFORNIA CRACKDOWN ON CHILD EXPLOITATION CRIMES

"Protecting children from sexual predators is a priority of the highest order," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva said. "We will continue to pursue this alleged offender and work with our law enforcement partners to return him to the United States to face trial for the crimes he is charged with committing."

FBI Criminal Assistant Director Heith Janke said Lang had been accused by multiple victims of sexually abusing minors.

FBI ANNOUNCES 305 ARRESTS, 24 MISSING CHILDREN RECOVERED IN CHICAGO DURING OPERATION NEW DAWN

"The FBI remains committed to identifying, investigating, and bringing offenders to justice who prey on some of the most vulnerable members of our communities," Janke said.

The FBI had offered a reward of up to $5,000 for information leading to Lang’s arrest and warned he should be considered an escape risk.

ALLEGED IRISH CARTEL BOSS ARRESTED IN COVERT OPERATION ON ORGANIZED CRIME CHARGES AFTER YEARS-LONG MANHUNT

Lang’s apprehension came through cooperation between the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police’s Pacific Region, authorities said. The RCMP’s Tofinoofino General Duty, Island District GIS, Nanaimo Detachment and Island District ERT assisted in the arrest, while the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs helped secure it.

If convicted in the Hawaii case, Lang faces a mandatory minimum of 15 years in prison and up to 30 years behind bars. He could also face a fine of up to $250,000 and supervised release of between five years and life.

UKRAINE UNLEASHES MORE THAN 400 DRONES NEAR MOSCOW IN ONE OF WAR'S BIGGEST ATTACKS

item.title: Big Ten bans NFL returnees, putting LSU and Lane Kiffin on collision course with the SEC
item.description: Big Ten's new rule bars players with NFL experience from eligibility as lawsuits and injunctions reshape the college football transfer landscape.
item.content:encoded:
The Big Ten has taken steps to prevent athletes who have signed NFL contracts from joining the conference this season — and in the future.

Following recent developments that have seen former college players enter the professional ranks, only to regain college eligibility through court orders, the conference voted Tuesday to bar those athletes moving forward.

Under the new Big Ten policy, any athlete who has signed with a professional team, declared for the NFL Draft or participated in any type of professional training camp will be ineligible for conference competition.

NFL TO NCAA? COURTROOM CHAOS IS GIVING PRO ATHLETES A BIZARRE PATH BACK TO COLLEGE, AND IT'S ONLY JUST BEGUN

The decision comes after players in several states were granted injunctions or temporary restraining orders allowing them to play this season.

Most of the lawsuits stem from the NCAA’s new eligibility guidelines, which give athletes five years to play five seasons of college athletics.

Since June, there have been a plethora of lawsuits filed in state courts that have granted athletes an additional season of eligibility, with multiple judges ruling in favor of plaintiffs that argued the NCAA's new rules should have included them being grandfathered into the process.

In recent days, LSU head coach Lane Kiffin has taken a beating in the court of public opinion, and from many within the SEC, for bringing back players who have already gained NFL experience.

This includes former Ole Miss football players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, who are both set to join the LSU roster thanks to a ruling from the 19th District Court of Louisiana that granted them an additional season of eligibility.

LSU’S LANE KIFFIN FIRES BACK AT NFL RETURNEE BACKLASH: BLAME THE NCAA, NOT US FOR RECRUITING PRO ATHLETES

But, there have been plenty others who have gone down this route, winning cases in state courts that allow them to return this season. Texas offensive lineman Cole Hutson is another, who sued the NCAA in a Texas court for an additional season.

In the SEC, there are meetings taking place over the next 24 hours that include Presidents, Chancellors and athletic directors. They are discussing their path forward, with a number of them in favor of the conference implementing the same rule as the Big Ten.

OREGON COACH DAN LANNING LAYS OUT MULTIPLE REASONS WHY NFL PLAYERS RETURNING TO COLLEGE FOOTBALL IS 'UNFAIR'

The problem is that LSU sees its own way around the conference ruling, thanks to a Louisiana court order.

If the conference were to start governing themselves more than normal, we could end up seeing a school like LSU testing the legal strength of a court order, by including the SEC in a lawsuit against the NCAA.

Officials from LSU will be in Birmingham, Alabama with their colleagues this week discussing the ongoing situation. A majority of SEC officials are against the idea of athletes with NFL experience returning to college, according to sources.

While the Tigers could back off their stance to take athletes from the NFL, head coach Lane Kiffin has essentially put his foot in the ground when it comes to this disagreement.

"So, you know, we have you know made a decision to recruit some kids around the country, and through these multiple injunctions around the country, which, this is not a first time in college sports, a group of players were granted a fifth year of eligibility, in multiple sports. And through them winning their injunction and entry into the portal, they’re available to recruit," Kiffin noted on Monday.

"So ourselves, like many places around the country, are recruiting them. At the end of the day, you know, because of these rulings, they’re either going to play for you or they’re going to play somewhere else around the country. So, we made a decision to recruit them, like probably most people are."

Will this turn into a legal battle within the SEC?

Sure, it could, if the Tigers administration feels as though it could win the court battle that could be lying ahead with its own conference.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

There are plenty of SEC officials who would like to see the conference go the same route as the Big Ten, with the ACC and Big 12 discussing their own path forward with a new rule.

Time will tell, but there seems to be a battle brewing in the Bayou.

And, it could involve a team deciding it is prepared to battle its own conference over a new rule.

item.title: Triathlete channels his inner 'Three Stooges' to escape harrowing alligator attack in South Carolina
item.description: Jonathan Bruney fought off a large alligator attack in South Carolina's Savannah River by gouging its eye during Ironman triathlon training.
item.content:encoded:
A triathlete got more than he bargained for when he went for a swim in a local South Carolina river in preparation for an Ironman competition next month.

Jonathan Bruney, 31, was training for an upcoming triathlon in the Savannah River on Sunday when he felt an unfamiliar but powerful pain in his arm.

"Out of nowhere, it hit me," Bruney told CBS affiliate WRDW. "It was a pretty big impact to my right side… it felt as if my elbow had made a hard impact, maybe like diving on a gym basketball court."

SON OF FLORIDA ALLIGATOR ATTACK VICTIM SAYS TOURISTS AND TIKTOKERS ARE EMBOLDENING THE GATORS

Bruney said he was swimming when he thought he hit a log at first, before pain started shooting up his entire arm confirming that something far more serious was afoot.

A large alligator had latched onto Bruney's right arm, and the endurance athlete suddenly went into survival mode.

"I immediately thought, ‘I need to get this off of me,’ because I didn’t want him to spin or death roll and do even more damage," Bruney explained.

Rather than panic, Bruney remembered a weak spot and acted almost instinctively.

SHARK WEEK PUTS SHARK BITE SURVIVAL IN FOCUS WITH ER DOC'S EXPERT TIPS

"I just knew the eyes were what you should target," Bruney said. "I put my hand on the snout, reached up, and pushed my thumb into his eyeball, and he released."

After he emerged from the water, Bruney was bleeding so profusely that a fellow triathlete (and first responder), Matthew Davis, had to use a cord from his swim buoy as a makeshift tourniquet, WRDW reported.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

After a bystander called 911, first responders were able to get Bruney to a local hospital, where doctors were able to determine that the injuries were treatable and not long-term in nature.

"It could have been a lot worse," Bruney told the outlet.

He added that although he doesn't fear the water after the incident, he now has a "healthy respect" for it, and still plans to compete in the Ironman triathlon next month.

item.title: Michigan Democrat awkwardly pivots to circumcision during heated Fox News debate on child sex changes

"Abdul, Michigan's not going for that. That is sick stuff," Watters responded before moving the conversation toward transgender athletes in women’s sports.

El-Sayed initially declined to answer the question, instead saying Watters had not asked about issues "people actually care about in Michigan," including groceries and healthcare.

"You don’t seem to want to talk about any of those things. You want to bring up all this culture war that, you know, I'm not here to fight a culture war, I’m here to fight the affordability crisis that people are facing," he added.

The pair later returned to transgender athletes in women’s sports, with El-Sayed saying the rules should be "decided by the people who govern sports."

REPUBLICANS GET THE DEMOCRAT THEY WANTED AS SOCIALIST ABDUL EL-SAYED WINS MICHIGAN SENATE PRIMARY

The tense exchange was part of a wide-ranging segment in which Watters and El-Sayed also went back and forth on wealth taxes, religious freedom and foreign policy, while El-Sayed repeatedly tried to shift focus to working-class economic concerns.

El-Sayed is the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s open U.S. Senate seat and is set to face Republican nominee Mike Rogers in November. He earned a doctorate in public health from Oxford University and a medical degree from Columbia University.

item.title: Taylor Fritz is dating Olivia Jade, Sunday Ticket is highway robbery & Dolly Parton's best sports moments
item.description: Taylor Fritz steps out with Olivia Jade, Sunday Ticket continues to gouge NFL fans and a look back on Dolly Parton's iconic Cowboys halftime show.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

I'm not a person who gets starstruck.

Maybe it's the line of work I'm in. Since college, I've spent my entire career working with professional athletes, including some of the biggest names in MLB and the NFL. And working in sports, I've crossed paths with countless other celebrities, too — actors, musicians, TV personalities.

I don't say that as some sort of not-so-humble brag. It's just a fact that even the biggest stars on the planet are still people, and none of them have ever really blown me away in real life.

Except one: Dolly Parton.

Back in 2016, devastating wildfires ripped through Gatlinburg, Tenn., burning more than 17,900 acres, damaging or destroying roughly 2,400 structures and killing 14 people.

In addition to donating her own money, Dolly established the My People Fund, which ultimately provided millions of dollars directly to families who lost their homes in the disaster. I ran social media for the Titans at the time, and a few of our players volunteered to answer phones during Dolly's telethon to help raise money for the victims.

I'll never forget walking into that studio and immediately being greeted by the blondest, biggest hair and the sparkliest rhinestones I'd ever seen.

"Thanks for coming," she said with a huge smile. "I'm Dolly!"

Folks, I could not breathe.

I could not believe this living legend was standing right in front of me, reaching out to shake my hand. How could someone so tiny be so... larger than life?

They say never to meet your heroes, but that wasn't true with Dolly. She couldn't have been kinder or more genuine. Everything I imagined her to be.

And the wildfire relief was just the tip of the iceberg for a woman who seemed to pour everything she had into the people and places she cared about.

Through the Dollywood Foundation, she created Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, which has mailed hundreds of millions of free books to young children around the world. She funded scholarships for local students, helped provide tuition assistance for Dollywood employees and donated millions of dollars to medical research at Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

That generosity wasn't some side project attached to her celebrity. It was part of who she was.

In the video announcing her death Tuesday, Dolly's nephew Bryan Seaver said, "She never saw a door she couldn't open, and the doors she opened made and changed history."

We can learn a lot from Dolly — how to treat our fellow human beings, how to show up for our communities and how to be so unapologetically true to ourselves that we don't give a damn what anyone has to say about it.

Dolly's music will live forever. But her legacy is so much bigger than the songs.

It's in the kids who learned to love reading because a book showed up in their mailbox. It's in the families who had somewhere to turn after losing everything. It's in the people she helped simply because she could.

And, selfishly, it'll always be in the memory of one dumbstruck 27-year-old standing in a television studio, temporarily forgetting how to breathe because Dolly Parton smiled, reached out her hand and said, "I'm Dolly."

What a gift she was.

We've made it, folks — the weekend you've all been waiting for.

You've had it in your calendars all year, you've sat around all summer desperately yearning for it to get here, counting the days and weeks as they slowly ticked by. And finally it's here.

The Bassmaster Elite at St. Lawrence River.

You thought I was going to say college football, didn't you? Well that, too! After a summer full of nauseating WNBA drama, that UNC-TCU kickoff in Dublin is gonna hit like crack. (As they say. I've never tried it.)

But I am very pumped about this fishing tournament, too. You may have noticed — as a part of our spiffy new rebrand — OutKick OutDoors is now an official arm of our website. And the St. Lawrence will be our first major event.

RANDY MOSS LAUNCHES YOUTUBE BASS FISHING SERIES WHILE HEADLINING RECORD $3.25M TOURNAMENT IN NASHVILLE

After the tournament, we'll be in a boat for the Randy Moss Pro-Am, where a bunch of Pro Football Hall of Famers will take on the top bass anglers in the country. It's going to be a hoot.

So make sure you're following us on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, and don't miss out, OK?!

Now that we have that out of the way, it's time to see what the internet is up to today. Grab your favorite cold beverage and settle in for your Tuesday 'Cap.

Look, I know Bobby wrote about this yesterday and it was a hot topic in our newsletter this morning. But I just cannot get over how expensive NFL Sunday Ticket is these days. $480! And for what?

I've had Sunday Ticket for years. I'm a Miami Dolphins fan (womp, womp), and — aside from illegal streams that would almost certainly fill my laptop with viruses — Sunday Ticket used to be the only way I could watch every Phins snap from my house in Middle Tennessee.

But this year, my husband and I had pretty much decided we weren't going to renew it.

So imagine our surprise when that $480 renewal fee hit the ol' bank account in EARLY JULY. YouTubeTV pulled a fast one, alright — slapping us with the auto-renewal a full two months before the season even starts.

Dirty.

So here I am again. Paying damn near $500 to watch my crappy football team play crappy football.

At least I won't have to deal with this dude anymore.

This sort of stuff was endearing when we were putting up 70 points on the Broncos. It got really old after Tua's 37th concussion.

Oh well, your problem now, Justin Herbert.

Who is Olivia Jade?

Thank you for asking. Olivia Jade is an influencer (because that's a job in the Year of our Lord 2026), but she's also Lori Loughlin's daughter.

Aunt Becky Jr., if you will.

She looks just like her, too.

The daughter who went to USC thanks to that big college admissions scandal?!

That very same one.

Anyway, she's bounced back and is now dating tennis star Taylor Fritz. But reps say they're just "taking things slow." Whatever that means in celebrity-speak.

Listen, summer is winding down (don't tell Joe Kinsey I said that), and love is in the air. We've got all these NFL WAGs petting their husbands and boyfriends at training camp. We've got golfer Wyndham Clark and Emily Tanner moving in together. We've got Bryson DeChambeau hard launching with Mikayla Demaiter.

And now Taylor and Olivia.

Cuffing season is right around the corner, single folks. Get on it.

Fly high, Dolly. There'll never be another one like you.

item.title: Trump mourns Dolly Parton, orders US flags lowered nationwide after country music icon dies
item.description: Trump ordered American flags lowered nationwide for one week in honor of Dolly Parton, calling her death "a true loss for millions of people."
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump ordered American flags lowered across the United States for one week Tuesday, as he mourned the death of country music icon Dolly Parton, telling the legendary singer, "The World loves you."

Parton died peacefully Tuesday in Nashville, Tennessee, according to an announcement shared by her representatives. She was 80.

"Very sad to report that Dolly Parton, one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER, has just passed away," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will."

DOLLY PARTON’S ONGOING HEALTH BATTLE FORCES COUNTRY LEGEND TO MISS MAJOR DOLLYWOOD EVENT

Trump then announced a presidential tribute to Parton.

"In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM," Trump wrote. "Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you."

Trump's tribute came as Parton's family and representatives remembered a woman whose influence stretched far beyond the country music stages that made her famous.

"A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family," the announcement said. "Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience."

DOLLY PARTON CANCELS LAS VEGAS RESIDENCY AS HEALTH ISSUES FORCE HER TO STEP BACK FROM STAGE PERFORMANCES

Parton, born Jan. 19, 1946, had a seven-decade career spanning music, songwriting, acting, writing and philanthropy.

She was preceded in death by her husband of 59 years, Carl Thomas Dean, who died in 2025, as well as her mother, Avie Lee Caroline Owens, and father, Robert Lee Parton Sr., according to the announcement.

DOLLY PARTON'S CALIFORNIA RETREAT WITH WIG ROOM AND DOLLYWOOD BIRDHOUSE LISTS FOR $1.95M

At Parton's request, a small, private service will be held for immediate family. Fans and friends were encouraged to pay tribute on social media or through Parton's official website.

In lieu of flowers, the family asked for donations to Dolly Parton's Imagination Library.

TAYLOR SWIFT'S VIDEO TRIBUTE TO ALAN JACKSON DIVIDES CROWD AT COUNTRY LEGEND'S FINAL SHOW

Parton's nephew and head of security, Bryan Seaver, also shared a video message following her death.

Tributes quickly poured in from Tennessee and across the country.

CARRIE UNDERWOOD, GARY SINISE LEAD STARS WHO'VE SHARED WHY THEY'RE PROUD TO BE AMERICANS

"There are no words to adequately express the sorrow our family and indeed, all Tennesseans, feel in the loss of Dolly Parton," Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., wrote on X. "An iconic leader who loved our great state and nation. Her passing leaves a void that no one can ever fill. Dolly, we will always love you."

House Republicans called Parton "an American icon" and "a national treasure," praising her as "a legendary artist, a generous philanthropist, and a proud daughter of Tennessee whose music and spirit touched generations of Americans."

SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM DEAD AT 71 AFTER 'BRIEF AND SUDDEN' ILLNESS, OFFICE SAYS

Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., remembered Parton as "an incredible East Tennessean" who "never changed her accent or forgot where she came from."

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott announced his state would also lower its flags in Parton's honor.

"So sad to lose this legend," Abbott wrote on X. "Texas will lower our flags in her honor. God Bless Dolly."

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said "America has lost a true national treasure," pointing to Parton's Tennessee roots, worldwide success and philanthropy.

"Dolly Parton’s unmistakable voice, joyful spirit, and remarkable generosity touched generations of Americans and many others around the world," Johnson wrote. "From the mountains of Tennessee to stages across the globe, she never forgot where she came from, and she used her extraordinary success to lift up countless others."

The Department of the Interior paid tribute to Parton's deep connection to her Tennessee roots and the Great Smoky Mountains.

"Dolly Parton carried the music, stories and spirit of her Tennessee mountain home wherever she went," the department said. "She was a lifelong champion of the Great Smoky Mountains and proudly shared her love for them with the world."

The Franklin Police Department also mourned the singer, saying her "roots and heart were always deeply connected to Tennessee."

Parton's family said the music and generosity that defined her extraordinary life would endure.

"Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages," the announcement said, "and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact."
